# 06 · Continue work without trusting a stale summary

## Start here

This lesson addresses an everyday problem: yesterday's assistant conversation ended, and today you want to continue. You do not need a memory plugin. First understand what the next conversation needs to know and what it must verify. [Evidence packets](04.md) provides the useful distinction between a fact, a source, and a hypothesis.

## The idea in plain language

In this course, **memory** means information retained for later use. It might be a short note, a file, or stored application state. That is different from the model's general learned knowledge. A fresh conversation should not be assumed to know earlier chat history, local files, or progress from another account.

A **handoff** tells the next session the goal, what has happened, what evidence exists, what remains uncertain, and the next useful step. A **checkpoint** records the state of work at a particular moment. For example, “test drafted, not run” is a meaningful checkpoint. “All done” is not meaningful unless the relevant result can be checked.

The problem is that memory becomes stale. A file may have changed since a note was written. A failed service may have recovered. A hypothesis repeated in a summary may begin to look like a fact. **Reconciliation** means comparing a stored claim with current evidence and resolving any disagreement. **Invalidation** means deciding that an old item needs rechecking because a relevant condition changed.

An SDET already encounters this distinction when a test report belongs to yesterday's build. A passing report for commit A does not establish that commit B passed. A good assistant handoff preserves the relationship between the report and the work it checked.

For a short explanation, persistent memory adds little. It matters for long investigations, unfinished coding work, repeated sessions, and account changes. Store only what supports those tasks; retaining complete private chat transcripts is not necessary for a useful project handoff.

## A small example

Here is an invented status for a search-sort investigation:

```text
Goal: explain why sorting test SORT-9 differs between two environments.
Observed: yesterday's run used build A and locale en-GB.
Hypothesis: locale changes the ordering; not tested yet.
Current change: the test environment now runs build B.
Next step: check build B's locale before comparing the sort behavior.
No new test result is available.
```

The hypothesis may still be useful, but yesterday's result is not evidence about build B. A good continuation retains the old observation as history and asks for the new configuration or run result. It does not silently convert “locale might explain it” into “locale was the confirmed cause.”

A saved path is also a claim that needs verification. A note saying “report exists at work/sort-report.txt” does not create that file. In this example no such file was supplied; the assistant should not pretend to read one.

## Try it with Codex or Claude Code

1. Open a new conversation in your existing assistant. The [quickstart](../../docs/ASSISTANT-QUICKSTART.md) explains the product entry points.
2. Paste the prompt below. It deliberately contains everything needed, so earlier conversations are irrelevant.
3. Inspect what the assistant treats as historical, current, and unverified. You can compare the reply with the example line by line.

```text
Teach safe continuation using only this synthetic handoff.
Goal: investigate SORT-9 ordering differences between two environments.
Yesterday's observation used build A and locale en-GB.
Hypothesis: locale changes ordering; untested.
Today the environment runs build B. Its locale and test result are unknown.
Explain what can be carried forward, what needs rechecking, and the first
useful next question. Do not claim a test ran or a report exists.
Then show a compact improved handoff in your reply, marking the hypothesis.
Do not create files or alter my learning progress.
```

If you later use this technique in the repository, ask the assistant to read the actual files referenced by a handoff before reporting their status. Keep a new note under a private location if it contains personal learning history. A project README can explain shared goals without storing your private attempts.

## What you should see

The reply should preserve yesterday's observation and its build identifier, mark the locale explanation as untested, and ask about today's environment. It should not declare the investigation complete. A concise handoff may be just a few sentences; the number of fields is less important than these distinctions.

You can continue to [tool contracts](07.md) when you understand why a stored summary helps resume work but does not replace checking reality. The academy's “Save my place” is a reading bookmark, not proof that you completed or mastered a topic.

## If it goes wrong

If the assistant says “as we established earlier,” ask which supplied evidence supports that statement. If it turns a hypothesis into a fact, point out the “untested” label. If it cannot access a referenced file, have it report that limitation and ask for the relevant excerpt rather than infer the file's contents.

If you change accounts, bring the project files and an explicit progress export or handoff. Do not expect the new login to inherit private browser storage or chats. The [continue-learning guide](../../docs/CONTINUE-LEARNING.md) and [local-data guide](../../docs/LOCAL-DATA.md) explain this academy's actual storage boundaries.

## Go deeper

Read **Compaction** and **Structured note-taking** within Anthropic's [Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents). Stop before **Sub-agent architectures**. Public reading; understanding context from lesson 04 is sufficient. Treat provider implementation details as examples, not promises about your current assistant. The sections were checked on 21 October 2026.

## Optional practice

Ask your tutor for a short handoff containing one stale claim. Identify what should be rechecked before receiving its answer. The [original memory lesson](../lessons/06-memory-and-handoffs.md) retains richer handoff and deletion-policy exercises. Its files are learner-created fixtures when you choose that practice; they are not prerequisites to reading this page.
